15980:
A threat is something that signals harm that has not happened yet — but could. That idea of potential, future harm is the beating heart of this word. Whether it comes from a person's mouth or from a gathering storm, a threat is always about what might happen, not what already has.

The word carries two distinct but closely related meanings, and a complete understanding of "threat" requires knowing both.
Meaning 1 — A Deliberate Statement of Intended Harm

In this sense, a threat is a deliberate communication — spoken, written, or implied — in which someone signals to another person that harm, punishment, or negative consequences will follow, usually unless certain conditions are met.

Think of it this way: someone is using the promise of future harm as a tool to intimidate, control, or coerce another person.

A few clear examples: "Give me the money, or I'll hurt you." A country declaring that it will strike back if its territory is invaded. A bully telling a classmate, "Tell anyone about this, and you'll regret it." All of these are threats in this first sense.

Notice the typical structure hiding inside these examples. There is often a condition — "if you do X, I will do Y to you" — though the condition is sometimes left unspoken and only implied. The key ingredients are: a person who intends to cause harm, a target at whom the threat is aimed, and a harm that is promised but hasn't been carried out yet.

Real vs. Empty Threats

Not all threats are genuine. An empty threat (also called an idle threat or a hollow threat) is a warning someone delivers but never actually intends to follow through on. A tired parent saying to a misbehaving child, "If you don't behave, we're cancelling the holiday," is almost certainly making an empty threat. The words carry the shape of a threat, but there is no real intention behind them. People often make empty threats out of frustration.

A threat that is followed through on is said to be carried out or followed through on. When we say someone "made good on their threat," we mean they actually did what they promised to do.

Some specific kinds of threat in this meaning: A death threat is a threat to kill someone. A bomb threat is a warning that an explosive device has been placed somewhere.

In this second sense, no one needs to say anything at all. Here, a threat simply refers to any person, thing, or situation that has the potential to cause harm, damage, or loss. The "threat" is a source of danger that exists in the world.

Examples make this crystal clear. "Climate change is a threat to the planet." Nobody is threatening the planet — climate change is simply a powerful force that could cause immense damage. "The rival company is a serious threat to our business." The rival hasn't said a word to anyone — it simply poses a danger to the other company's survival. "The infected water supply is a threat to public health." The water doesn't have intentions — it is just a source of potential harm.

This is the sense you encounter when people talk about national security threats, environmental threats, health threats, or existential threats. In all of these cases, something dangerous exists and could cause harm — that's the threat.

Despite seeming different on the surface, both meanings share the same essential core: a source of harm that is real or likely, but hasn't struck yet. Whether it is a criminal saying "cross me and you'll pay," or a wildfire approaching a town, the common thread is impending potential harm. The first meaning focuses on human intention and communication; the second focuses purely on the danger itself.

Threat vs. Warning

A warning is given to protect someone — it tells them that danger exists so they can avoid it. A threat, in the first sense, is given to control someone — the speaker is the source of the danger. A doctor who says "smoking will kill you" is giving a warning. An attacker who says "hand over your wallet or I'll hurt you" is making a threat. The key difference is whose side the speaker is on: a warning-giver is trying to help you; a threat-maker is the one you need to be afraid of.

Threat vs. Danger

In the second meaning, these two words are close cousins, but "danger" tends to describe a situation that is already present and immediate, while "threat" implies an active source — something that could strike, attack, or cause damage. A shark in the water right next to you is a danger. A shark spotted in the general area is a threat.

Threat vs. Risk

"Risk" is more about the probability that something bad will happen. "Threat" is more about the active source of that potential harm. Slippery floors are a risk. A tiger on the loose is a threat.

These are the most important phrases built around the word "threat" that you will encounter in real English:

Pose a threat (to something/someone) — to represent a danger. "The disease poses a serious threat to elderly populations."

Under threat — in danger of being harmed, destroyed, or lost. "Many species of birds are currently under threat." "The old library is under threat of demolition."

Make/issue a threat — to deliver a threat to someone.

Carry out a threat / follow through on a threat — to actually do what was threatened.

Face a threat — to be confronted with a danger.

A real/serious/major threat — a genuine and significant danger.

An empty/idle/hollow threat — a threat with no real intention behind it.

The noun "threat" means either (1) a deliberate statement or communication in which someone promises harm to another person in order to intimidate or control them, or (2) any person, thing, or situation that is a source of potential harm or danger to something or someone. In both cases, the defining feature of a threat is that the harm is possible or probable, but not yet realized. The moment the harm actually occurs, it is no longer a threat — it has become an attack, a disaster, or damage. A threat always lives in the space between now and what could happen next.
15981: "Threaten" means to signal that something bad, harmful, or dangerous may happen — either because a person deliberately intends to cause it, or because a situation is naturally moving toward it. Whenever this word appears, something harmful is either being promised, looming in the background, or drawing dangerously close.

Sense 1 — A Person Warns Another Person of Harm

This is the sense most people know first. When one person threatens another, they communicate — through spoken words, a written message, or even a physical gesture — that they will do something harmful. The purpose is usually to scare the other person, pressure them into doing something, or show power over them.

The critical ingredient here is intent. A real person is deliberately choosing to make someone else feel fear or pressure.

For example: "He threatened to report her to the police unless she returned the money." Here, he is using the possibility of harm as a weapon to get what he wants. Or: "The gang members threatened witnesses before the trial began." Here, the purpose is pure intimidation — to silence people through fear.

You will often see this structure: threaten + to + verb. "She threatened to quit." "He threatened to expose the truth." "They threatened to sue the company." In each case, a person is saying, in effect, "Do what I want — or else this bad thing will happen."

You will also commonly see: threaten someone with something. "He threatened her with violence." "The manager threatened the employees with termination." Here, the harmful thing is stated as a noun rather than an action.

And sometimes it appears as: threaten that + a full sentence. "He threatened that he would destroy her reputation." This works exactly the same way, just with a fuller description of the intended harm.

One important thing to note: the threat does not have to be carried out for the word to apply. The moment someone signals harmful intent, the act of threatening has occurred. Whether they follow through is a separate matter.

Sense 2 — Something (Not a Person) Poses Danger to Something Else

This is a broader and very important use of the word. Here, the subject doing the "threatening" is not a person with a plan — it is a force, situation, or phenomenon that puts something at risk.

For example: "Rising sea levels threaten coastal cities." The sea has no intention. It is not angry, and it is not trying to pressure anyone. But it still threatens — meaning it puts those cities in danger of being harmed or destroyed.

More examples in the same pattern: "The drought threatens the nation's food supply." "Deforestation threatens the survival of many species." "The virus threatened millions of lives."

Notice the structure here: something threatens something else. The first "something" is the source of danger (drought, deforestation, a disease). The second "something" is what is at risk (food supply, species, lives). There is no human intent involved — just the natural force of one thing endangering another.

This sense is extremely common in news writing, science, and formal discussion.

Sense 3 — Something Bad Seems About to Happen

In this third sense, "threaten" describes a situation that looks like it is heading toward a bad outcome. Think of it as the verb form of "on the verge of something unwanted."

For example: "The argument threatened to turn violent." This means the argument was moving in a direction where violence seemed likely — it hadn't happened yet, but the signs were there. Or: "What began as a small disagreement threatened to become a full-blown crisis." Or: "The project threatened to go over budget."

The structure here is almost always: something threatens to + verb. The thing doing the threatening is a situation, and what it "threatens to do" is the bad outcome approaching.

This sense is closely related to Sense 2, but the subtle difference is that Sense 2 says something is already a source of danger ("droughts threaten crops"), while Sense 3 emphasizes that something bad is about to unfold ("the situation threatened to collapse").

This is worth knowing on its own because it works differently. When you say someone feels threatened, you are describing their emotional state — a feeling of fear, insecurity, or sensing that their safety, status, or wellbeing is in danger. Crucially, nobody necessarily needs to have said anything threatening for this to apply.

For example: "She felt threatened by his aggressive tone." He may not have said "I will hurt you" — but his manner made her feel unsafe. Or: "Some managers feel threatened by employees who are smarter than them." Here, no actual physical danger exists — it is a feeling of one's position or importance being at risk.

This expression captures a psychological experience of threat, not just a literal one.

Threats can be explicit or implied. An explicit threat is stated clearly: "I will hurt you if you don't cooperate." An implied threat uses actions, tone, or situation to communicate the same danger without saying it directly — for example, someone slowly sharpening a knife while staring at you, or a gang standing outside someone's house. "Threaten" covers both.

The word always carries a negative weight. You will never use "threaten" to describe something good that is approaching. It is always tied to harm, danger, loss, or an unwanted outcome.

The subject can be a person, an object, a situation, or a natural force. A criminal can threaten you. A storm can threaten a town. A conflict can threaten peace. The word is flexible in its subject, but what remains constant is the idea of imminent harm or danger.

"Threaten" is often used in the passive voice. "She was threatened at gunpoint." "Endangered animals are threatened by habitat destruction." "He felt he was being threatened." In passive constructions, the focus shifts to the person or thing being endangered, rather than the source of the threat.

Think of "threaten" as a word that lives at the intersection of danger and anticipation. Something harmful has not necessarily happened yet — but it is being promised, it is looming, or it is building up momentum. Whether a person is using words to intimidate another, a disease is putting a population at risk, or a negotiation is on the verge of breaking down completely — in all of these cases, "threaten" is the right word, because in each one, something bad is either being signaled or is drawing close.

If you can hold onto one simple idea, let it be this: to threaten is to bring harm — real or possible, intended or natural — dangerously close to someone or something.
15982:
Threatened means: in a state of danger, or perceiving oneself to be in danger.

It describes the condition of something — a person, an animal, a species, a feeling, an idea — that is at risk of being harmed, destroyed, or taken away.

"Threatened" as an adjective has two distinct uses. Both share the same underlying idea (being at risk), but they apply in different contexts.

Meaning 1 — Emotional / Psychological

This is the most everyday use. A person (or an animal) feels threatened when they sense danger — whether real or imagined. It describes an internal feeling of being unsafe, insecure, or under attack.

This "danger" is very often not physical. It is frequently a danger to one's:

  • Status or position ("He felt threatened when a smarter colleague joined the team.")
  • Self-esteem or ego ("Criticism made her feel threatened.")
  • Relationships ("He became cold and distant — classic signs of a threatened person who fears rejection.")
  • Authority ("The manager felt threatened by employees who questioned her decisions.")
  • Sense of security ("Children who grow up in unstable homes often develop a threatened sense of self.")

A key point: when someone feels threatened, it does not necessarily mean actual danger exists. It only means they perceive a risk. Someone can feel threatened by a compliment if they interpret it as a challenge.

This is why the word is so widely used in psychology, relationships, and everyday conversation. It captures that uneasy, defensive, on-edge feeling when you sense that something important to you might be lost or attacked.

Meaning 2 — Biological / Conservation

In science and conservation, threatened is a formal term. A threatened species is one that faces a serious risk of extinction — it is in danger of disappearing from the Earth if the conditions causing its decline are not addressed.

It sits on a spectrum of risk:

  • Least Concern → Near Threatened → Vulnerable → Endangered → Critically Endangered → Extinct in the Wild → Extinct

"Threatened" in formal conservation language is often used as an umbrella term covering Vulnerable, Endangered, and Critically Endangered together — essentially, any species that is in genuine danger of extinction.

Examples:

  • "The snow leopard is a threatened species."
  • "Many threatened plants rely on a single pollinator that is itself disappearing."
  • "Conservation efforts have brought some threatened populations back from the brink."

These two words are easy to confuse, so it's worth being clear:

WordWhat it describes
ThreateningSomething causing fear or danger — it is the source of threat
ThreatenedSomething experiencing fear or danger — it is on the receiving end
  • A threatening dog bares its teeth and growls — it is making others feel unsafe.
  • A threatened dog backs into a corner — it feels unsafe itself.

Both words can apply to the same situation from different angles. A lion that is threatened by hunters may become threatening in return. The first word describes its inner state; the second describes how it appears to others.

1. The feeling can be irrational.
You can feel threatened without any real danger being present. Insecurity, past trauma, or low confidence can all cause someone to feel threatened in perfectly safe situations. This is why you'll often see the phrase "feel threatened" rather than "be threatened" in everyday use — it acknowledges that the feeling is subjective.

2. The word applies to abstract things too.
It is not just people or species that can be threatened. Ideas, values, systems, and institutions can be described this way:

  • "Freedom of speech is threatened in many countries."
  • "Democracy feels threatened when powerful groups undermine elections."
  • "Their way of life felt threatened by rapid change."

In each case, something valued is at risk of being damaged or lost.

3. Degree matters.
Something can be mildly threatened or severely threatened. The word itself doesn't tell you how serious the danger is — context does. A species "mildly threatened" by habitat loss is in a very different situation from one "critically threatened" with only 50 individuals left.

4. It implies vulnerability.
There is an inherent vulnerability in the word. A "threatened" thing is not powerful in that moment — it is exposed, at risk, susceptible. This is why the word often carries an emotional weight, a sense of something fragile being in harm's way.

Threatened (adjective) means:

In a state of risk or danger — either felt internally (as a psychological state of insecurity or perceived danger) or existing externally (as a formal recognition that a species or thing faces the genuine risk of destruction or extinction).

If you remember one image: picture something valuable, cornered, with danger closing in. That thing — whether a nervous person in a tense meeting, or a rare bird losing its last forest — is threatened.
15983:
A threnody is a song, poem, or piece of music created specifically to mourn someone's death. Think of it as grief given artistic form — a structured, deliberate expression of sorrow composed in honour of a person or group of people who have died.

The word almost always refers to something created in response to death, not just felt. It is not the cry of grief itself; it is the art born from that grief.

A threnody has a few defining qualities:

It is about death, specifically. A threnody is not written about disappointment, failure, or general sadness. It is anchored to loss through death — the death of a specific person, or sometimes a larger group of people lost in a tragedy.

It is a formal artistic work. Anyone can weep. But a threnody is crafted — structured as a poem, composed as a piece of music, or written as a song. This is what separates a threnody from simply expressing grief out loud.

It mourns and honours at the same time. A threnody is not merely dark or despairing. It carries a sense of tribute. The act of creating one says: this person's death mattered enough that I will shape my sorrow into something that lasts.

It can be purely musical. Unlike a poem, a threnody does not have to contain words at all. An instrumental piece written to grieve a death is equally a threnody.

A threnody feels heavy, aching, and sorrowful — but also often beautiful, because the grief has been transformed into something artistic. Listening to or reading a threnody does not make you feel excitement or joy. It makes you feel a quiet, deep sadness — the kind that also carries reverence for the person being mourned. It is mournful in a dignified, composed way, not a raw or chaotic way.

Poets write threnodies when someone they love — or someone the world has lost — dies and the loss feels too large for ordinary words. Composers write threnodies when they want music to carry grief that language alone cannot express. The purpose is twofold: to process the grief of the creator, and to give others a shared space in which to grieve too.

A threnody can be private (a poet writing about a dead friend) or public (a composer writing for victims of a war or disaster).

One of the most celebrated threnodies in literature is the poem simply titled "Threnody" by the American poet Ralph Waldo Emerson, written after the death of his five-year-old son, Waldo, in 1842. It is raw, devastating, and profound — a father's artistic response to unbearable loss.

In music, Krzysztof Penderecki's Threnody for the Victims of Hiroshima (1960) is one of the most famous examples. Despite its title, Penderecki actually named it a threnody after composing it, when he realised the piece's deeply mournful character suited the word perfectly. It is written for 52 string instruments and sounds unlike conventional music — dissonant, anguished, and haunting. It mourns the tens of thousands killed in the atomic bombing of Hiroshima.

These examples show the range of the word: a threnody can mourn one person or thousands, can be intimate or sweeping, verbal or purely musical.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are close relatives of threnody, but they are not identical:

Elegy is perhaps the most commonly confused with threnody. An elegy is a poem written in a reflective, sorrowful tone — often about death, but not always. An elegy can mourn the loss of youth, time, a way of life, or even a living person's faded glory. A threnody is more specifically and strictly tied to actual death, and it carries a more directly lamenting, wailing quality. All threnodies in poetry are elegies in a broad sense, but not all elegies are threnodies.

Dirge refers specifically to a slow, mournful piece of music traditionally performed at or for a funeral. A dirge is almost always musical, and it is closely tied to the burial ceremony itself. A threnody can be performed at any time — years after a death — and exists as an independent artistic work, not just a ceremonial one.

Requiem is a religious musical composition based on the Roman Catholic Mass for the Dead. It is structured around specific prayers for the souls of the departed. A threnody has no religious structure or requirement — it is secular in nature and is simply defined by its mournful, lamenting character.

Lament is the broadest of these words. A lament is any expression of grief or sorrow — spoken, sung, written, or even just felt. A threnody is a specific, polished artistic form of lament. Think of lament as the raw emotion, and threnody as what a skilled artist does with that emotion.

Occasionally, writers use threnody in a looser, figurative sense to mean any long, sorrowful expression of loss — even when death is not literally involved. For example: "His memoir was a threnody for a childhood that had vanished." Here, the word is being used poetically to evoke the depth and formal quality of the grief, not to say someone literally died. However, this is a secondary, figurative use. In its primary and most accurate sense, a threnody is always rooted in death.

• The composer spent three months writing a threnody for his late mother, which was performed at a concert held in her memory.
  • Penderecki's threnody is considered one of the most emotionally powerful orchestral works of the twentieth century.
  • The anthology opens with a threnody — a heartbreaking poem written by a soldier who lost his closest friend in battle.
  • She described the novel as a kind of threnody, a sustained lamentation for an entire generation lost to war.
A threnody is a song, poem, or piece of music written to formally mourn and lament the death of a person or people — grief transformed into art.
15984:
To thresh means to beat harvested grain crops repeatedly in order to knock the edible seeds loose from the parts of the plant you cannot eat — the stalks, husks, and straw.

That's the heart of it. Everything else below is just this idea made clearer and fuller.

Picture a farmer who has just cut down a field of wheat. Each wheat plant is a tall stalk with small, edible seeds clustered at the top. Those seeds are the whole point — ground into flour, cooked as food, stored for winter. But the seeds don't just fall off. They sit tightly inside a protective shell, bound to the stalk. You have to force them free.

That forcing is threshing.

The farmer gathers cut stalks into bundles and beats them — against a hard floor, against a wooden post, or using a hand tool called a flail (two wooden sticks joined by a chain or rope, used like a whip). Each blow sends the seeds flying off the stalk and falling onto the floor below. After threshing, you end up with a heap of loose grain mixed with broken bits of stalk and papery husks — this light, airy waste is called chaff.

The grain and chaff are then separated in the next step called winnowing — but that's a separate process. Threshing is specifically the beating-to-separate step.
The physical quality of the action

The defining physical character of threshing is a repeated, forceful, flailing or striking motion. It is not a single blow — it is many blows, over and over, until all the seeds are knocked free. It is hard, rhythmic, physical work.

Threshing could be done several ways depending on the era and culture:

  • By hand with a flail — the classic method, where workers swing the flail and beat bundled stalks laid out on the ground.
  • By treading animals — oxen, horses, or donkeys were walked in circles over spread-out grain, their hooves crushing the seeds free from the stalks.
  • By a threshing machine (a thresher) — a large mechanical device that takes in bundles of grain crop, beats and shakes them internally, and delivers separated grain out of one end and straw out of the other. These machines transformed farming in the 18th and 19th centuries.

The place where hand-threshing was traditionally done is called a threshing floor — a broad, flat, very hard surface (stone or packed earth) designed so grain could be beaten cleanly without getting lost in soft ground.
Where the word appears most often

You will encounter "thresh" almost exclusively in contexts related to:

  • Agriculture, farming, and rural life — describing the actual process of separating grain crops. ("They spent three days threshing the harvest.")
  • Historical or traditional settings — the Bible, ancient literature, historical fiction, accounts of pre-industrial farming. Threshing was one of the central events of the agricultural year for thousands of years across nearly every grain-growing civilization on earth.
  • Agricultural machinery — the words thresher and threshing machine appear in writing about farm equipment and the history of mechanized farming.
The secondary meaning: wild, uncontrolled movement

Because threshing involves rapid, whipping, flailing motions, the word has at times been used to describe any vigorous, uncontrolled flailing of limbs or the whole body — a person thrashing in pain, arms flailing wildly, a fish flopping on the deck of a boat.

However — and this is important — this sense is rare with "thresh" in modern English. The closely related word "thrash" has almost entirely taken over this meaning. If you want to describe wild, uncontrolled movement today, "thrash" is the natural, modern word. "Thresh" in this flailing sense appears mostly in older writing or in poetic contexts where the author wants to deliberately echo the image of beating grain.

So in practice: thresh = grain separation (always correct); thresh = wild movement (you may encounter it in older texts, but "thrash" is the modern standard for that).

Grain-separation meaning (primary):

  • "Before machines existed, entire villages would come together to thresh the wheat after harvest."
  • "She watched the workers thresh the rice by beating bundled stalks against the rim of a large wooden tub."
  • "The invention of the mechanical thresher meant one machine could do in an hour what had taken twenty workers all day."
  • "The threshing floor was swept clean before the barley was spread out to be beaten."

Flailing-movement meaning (secondary/older):

  • "The great fish threshed desperately at the end of the line." (older/literary style — today, most writers would use "thrashed")

• Threshing (noun / present participle): "Threshing was the hardest work of the harvest season." / "They were threshing the barley."
  • Threshed (past tense): "By evening, they had threshed the entire field."
  • Thresher (noun): a person who threshes, or a machine built for threshing.
  • Threshing floor (noun): the hard, flat surface where threshing is done.
  • Threshing machine / thresher (noun): the mechanical device that separates grain from stalks automatically.
A quick summary to lock it in

Thresh = to beat harvested grain plants repeatedly so the edible seeds separate from the stalks, husks, and straw. The core image is force applied again and again — beating, flailing, striking — to get something loose and free from what surrounds it. It is ancient, physical, agricultural work, and the word carries all of that weight with it.
15985:
Before diving into the different meanings, here is the one idea that ties all of them together:

A threshold is the exact point where you cross from one state into another. It is the dividing line. The tipping point. The moment or place where "before" ends and "after" begins. Hold onto that idea, because every meaning of this word — whether physical, figurative, or scientific — is built on it.

In its most concrete, tangible sense, a threshold is the strip of flooring or the slab at the bottom of a doorway — the thing you literally step over when you walk through a door. It marks the boundary between one space and another: outside and inside, the hallway and the room, the street and the building.

By extension, the word also refers to the doorway or entrance itself, not just the strip on the floor. So when someone says "she stood at the threshold," they mean she was standing right at the entrance of a door — on the boundary between two spaces, having not yet fully stepped into either one.

He carried her over the threshold on their wedding day.
The cat sat at the threshold, deciding whether to go in or out.
Meaning 2: The Beginning of Something New

This is where the word grows beyond the physical and becomes powerful in everyday language. A threshold is the point at which something new begins — especially something significant, important, or life-changing.

Just like a doorway separates "outside" from "inside," a threshold in this sense separates what came before from what comes next. You are standing on the edge of something new. You haven't fully entered it yet, but you are right there, at the beginning of it.

She stood on the threshold of adulthood.
The country was on the threshold of a great revolution.
He felt that he was at the threshold of the most important chapter of his life.

Notice the phrase "on the threshold of" — it signals that something is just about to begin, or has just barely begun. It carries a sense of anticipation, of standing at a door that is about to open.
Meaning 3: The Minimum Level That Triggers Something

This is perhaps the most widely used meaning in science, medicine, psychology, and everyday practical life. Here, a threshold is the minimum level, point, or amount that is needed for something to happen, be felt, or take effect. If you are below the threshold, nothing happens. The moment you reach or cross it, something changes.

Think of it like a light switch. Nothing happens until your finger applies just enough pressure — and the moment it does, the light comes on. That exact point of "just enough" is the threshold.

Some examples will make this very clear:

Pain threshold: Every person has a different pain threshold — the level of pain at which they actually start to feel it as painful. Someone with a high pain threshold can tolerate a lot before it feels unbearable. Someone with a low pain threshold feels pain much more easily and quickly.

She has a very low pain threshold — even a small cut makes her wince.
Athletes often develop a higher pain threshold through training.

Hearing threshold: The minimum level of sound that a person's ears can detect. Sounds below this level are simply not heard.

Tax threshold / earnings threshold: In practical life, a threshold is often a specific number or level that, once crossed, changes what rules apply to you. A tax threshold, for example, is the income level at which you start paying a certain tax. Earn below it — you pay nothing. Earn above it — you pay.

Her salary just crossed the tax threshold this year.
The drug has no effect below a certain threshold dose.

Threshold in psychology: In the study of the mind, a threshold refers to the level at which a stimulus (something your senses detect) is just barely strong enough to be noticed consciously. Below the threshold, your brain doesn't register it. At or above the threshold, it does.

The signal was below the threshold of conscious awareness.

"On the threshold of" — about to enter or begin something; right at the start of a new phase.

We are on the threshold of a scientific breakthrough.

"Cross a threshold" — to pass a critical point after which things change; to move from one state to another.

Once the temperature crosses a certain threshold, the chemical reaction begins.

"Above/below the threshold" — whether something is strong enough, large enough, or significant enough to trigger an effect.

The noise was below the threshold of what the microphone could pick up.

"A threshold moment" — a turning point; a moment that marks the end of one era and the beginning of another.

Winning that award was a threshold moment in her career.
How to Know Which Meaning Is Being Used

The context will always tell you. If someone is talking about a doorway, a building, or a physical space, it's the literal meaning. If someone is talking about life events, history, or big changes, it's the "beginning of something new" meaning. If someone is talking about measurements, levels, science, medicine, taxes, or any kind of "amount that triggers a change," it's the "minimum level" meaning.
The One Sentence That Holds It All

No matter which meaning you encounter, a threshold is always the exact point where crossing it means you have moved from one state of being into another. It is the line between two worlds — the doorway between "not yet" and "now."
15986:
Thrift means the careful, wise, and deliberate management of money and resources so that as little as possible is wasted and as much as possible is saved.

A person who practices thrift doesn't spend money carelessly. They think before they buy. They save rather than splurge. They get the most value out of everything they have. Thrift is essentially the habit of living within your means and treating every penny as something worth respecting.

Think of it this way: if you earn $1,000 a month, spend $700, and save $300 — and you do this not out of poverty but out of discipline and good sense — that is thrift. You are practising thrift.
What Makes Thrift Special (Its Tone and Feel)

This is important: thrift is a positive word. It carries a sense of admiration and respect.

When you call someone thrifty, you are not insulting them. You are saying they are smart, disciplined, and sensible with money. Thrift is considered a virtue — a good quality of character — in most cultures. It suggests wisdom, not weakness.

This is what separates it from words that sound similar but feel different:

  • Stingy / miserly — these are negative words. A stingy person refuses to spend money even when it is reasonable or kind to do so. They hoard money out of selfishness or greed.
  • Cheap — often used negatively too; someone who avoids spending at the expense of quality, generosity, or fairness.
  • Thrifty / thrift — positive. The person is careful and wise, not selfish. They avoid waste, not generosity.

So the difference is about motivation and judgment. A thrifty person avoids unnecessary spending. A stingy person avoids all spending, even necessary or kind spending. Thrift is balance; miserliness is excess.
The Full Range of What Thrift Covers

While thrift is most commonly about money, the word can extend to the careful use of any resource — food, time, materials, energy, and so on.

For example:

  • Finishing all the food on your plate instead of throwing it away = thrift.
  • Reusing a container instead of buying a new one = thrift.
  • Using every scrap of fabric when sewing, so nothing is wasted = thrift.

The common thread is: don't waste what you have.

Here are some natural examples to help you see how the word is used:

  • "Her grandmother lived through hard times and learned the value of thrift early in life."
  • "The success of the small business was largely due to the owner's thrift and careful planning."
  • "Thrift, not luck, is what allowed him to retire at fifty."
  • "She bought furniture with great thrift — always choosing quality items at low prices from sales and second-hand shops."

Notice that in all these cases, thrift is something to be admired.
Other Specific Meanings of Thrift (as a Noun)

The word "thrift" also appears in a few specific, concrete contexts beyond its general meaning:

1. A Thrift Store (or Thrift Shop)
This is a shop — very common in the United States — that sells second-hand or donated goods (clothes, furniture, books, etc.) at very low prices. The word "thrift" is used here because shopping at such a store is itself an act of thrift: you get what you need without spending much. The word "thrift" in "thrift store" is used as a modifier (describing the type of store), but the noun "thrift" is the root of it.

People sometimes simply say, "I bought this at the thrift" — using "thrift" as a shortened noun for the store itself.

2. A Thrift (Financial Institution)
In financial and banking language, especially in the United States, a "thrift" (also called a thrift institution or savings institution) is a type of bank — specifically a savings bank or a savings-and-loan association — whose original purpose was to encourage ordinary people to save money. The name itself comes from the idea of promoting thrift (saving habits) among the public.

Example: "The community thrift offered higher interest rates on savings accounts than the big banks."

3. Thrift (the Plant)
"Thrift" is also the common name for a small flowering plant (Armeria maritima), often called sea thrift or sea pink. It grows in rocky, coastal areas and produces round clusters of pink or white flowers. It earned this name because it "thrives" in tough, sparse conditions with very little — a poetic nod to the idea of making the most of scarce resources. This is a specialised botanical use.
The Big Picture — How to Remember It

If you want one clear sentence to anchor everything: Thrift is the admirable habit of not wasting money or resources — spending wisely, saving consistently, and getting the most out of what you have.

It is a word rooted in discipline, wisdom, and good character. Whether it describes a person's habits, a type of store, a kind of bank, or a hardy little plant — in every case, the spirit of the word is the same: doing more with less, and doing it well.
15987:
Thrifty means being careful and smart about how you spend money. A thrifty person avoids wasting money, looks for good value, and thinks before spending. They don't buy things impulsively or carelessly — they plan, compare, and make wise choices so that their money goes as far as possible.

Think of it this way: a thrifty person sees money as a resource not to be wasted, just like a good cook sees food — they use every bit wisely and throw nothing away unnecessarily.

This is important: thrifty is a positive word. When you call someone thrifty, you are giving them a compliment. You are saying they are disciplined, smart, and responsible with money. The word carries a sense of admiration and respect.

This makes it different from words like cheap or stingy, which are negative and suggest someone is unreasonably unwilling to spend money, even when they should — for example, refusing to tip a waiter, or never buying gifts for anyone. A thrifty person, by contrast, is not selfish or ungenerous. They simply don't waste money. They spend it — but wisely.
What a Thrifty Person Actually Does

To make this concrete, here is what thrifty behaviour looks like in real life:

  • They wait for a sale before buying something they don't urgently need.
  • They cook at home more often instead of eating out frequently.
  • They repair broken things instead of immediately replacing them.
  • They compare prices before making a purchase.
  • They avoid buying things just because they are fashionable or impressive.
  • They save a portion of their income regularly.
  • They reuse and recycle items whenever possible.

None of this means they live miserably or never enjoy life. It just means they are intentional — every spending decision is made with thought.
The Spectrum: From Thrifty to Its Extremes

It helps to understand thrifty by placing it on a spectrum:

Extravagant → Moderate → Thrifty → Frugal → Stingy/Miserly

  • Extravagant people spend money freely, often excessively, without much care.
  • A moderate person spends normally — neither too freely nor too carefully.
  • A thrifty person is careful and wise, but still lives comfortably and reasonably.
  • A frugal person takes it a step further — cutting expenses to a minimum and living very simply. Frugal is slightly more intense than thrifty, with a stronger emphasis on avoiding all unnecessary costs.
  • A stingy or miserly person refuses to spend money even when it is reasonable or necessary to do so, and this becomes a fault that affects others negatively.

So thrifty sits in a sweet spot — careful enough to be admirable, but not so extreme that it becomes a problem.

These will help you see how the word feels in natural use:

  • "My grandmother was very thrifty — she never bought anything at full price if she could help it."
  • "Living on a small salary, he became quite thrifty and managed to save a surprising amount each month."
  • "She has a thrifty nature, always finding clever ways to stretch her budget."
  • "Being thrifty doesn't mean being unhappy — it means being smart with what you have."
  • "The thrifty couple paid off their mortgage in just ten years."

Since you are a learner, it helps to know how this word changes form:

  • Thrifty — adjective (She is thrifty.)
  • Thriftier / Thriftiest — comparative and superlative forms (He is thriftier than his brother. She is the thriftiest person I know.)
  • Thriftily — adverb (They lived thriftily for years to save up for a home.)
  • Thriftiness — noun referring to the quality or habit (Her thriftiness is what allowed her to retire early.)
  • Thrift — the core noun form (Thrift is a virtue that many people admire.)

These words are close in meaning to thrifty, but each has a slightly different shade:

  • Economical — focused on avoiding waste and getting good value; can apply to things, not just people (e.g., an economical car uses less fuel).
  • Frugal — similar to thrifty but slightly more extreme; implies a simpler lifestyle with minimal spending.
  • Prudent — wise and careful in general, not just with money; broader in scope.
  • Careful — very general; just means paying attention; lacks the specific financial meaning of thrifty.

Among all of these, thrifty is the word that most warmly and directly praises someone's wise money habits in everyday life.

• Wasteful — spending or using more than is needed.
  • Extravagant — spending excessively, often on luxury or show.
  • Spendthrift — a person who spends money recklessly and without care (note: spendthrift is the direct opposite of thrifty as a personality description).
  • Lavish — very generous or excessive in spending.
  • Prodigal — recklessly wasteful, especially of money (more formal/literary).

Thrifty is about respect for resources. A thrifty person understands that money represents time, effort, and energy — and so they don't let it slip away carelessly. They are not afraid to spend, but they are unwilling to waste. This quality is widely seen as a sign of maturity, self-control, and wisdom — which is exactly why the word carries such a positive tone wherever it is used.
15988:
A thrill is a sudden, strong, and intense feeling of excitement or pleasure — one that you experience not just in your mind, but physically in your body too. It is a wave of powerful feeling that hits you all at once, moves through you briefly, and leaves you feeling energized, alive, or deeply moved.

Three qualities define a thrill perfectly: it is sudden (it doesn't build slowly — it hits you), it is intense (it is never mild or faint), and it is brief (it lasts for a moment, not hours). It is a peak feeling, like a spike on a graph.

Example: "When she heard her name called as the winner, she felt a thrill run through her entire body."
The physical dimension — what makes thrill special

What separates a thrill from most other emotional words is that it is deeply physical. When you experience a thrill, your body reacts. You might feel a tingling or shivering sensation on your skin, a flutter in your chest or stomach, a rush of warmth, or even a brief weakness in your knees. This is why people often say a thrill "runs through" them or "goes down their spine" — because the feeling literally seems to travel through the body.

This physical quality is central to the word. Without that bodily sensation, it would just be called excitement or happiness. A thrill is the moment your body and emotions react together, at the same time, with full force.

Example: "A thrill of cold fear shot through him when he heard the strange noise behind him."

A thrill can be triggered by a wide range of experiences — anything that creates a sudden surge of strong feeling. Common causes include:

Achieving something difficult or unexpected (winning a competition, getting great news), experiencing something dangerous but safe enough to enjoy (a roller coaster, skydiving, a horror film), witnessing something breathtaking (a stunning musical performance, a spectacular sunset), being surprised by something wonderful, or even experiencing a moment of real danger. The thing that causes a thrill is usually something out of the ordinary — something that breaks the calmness of everyday life.

Example: "Seeing his favourite band perform live gave him the thrill of his life."
The "good fear" quality of a thrill

This is one of the most interesting and nuanced things about this word. A thrill does not always come from purely pleasant things. It can also come from fear, danger, or risk — but crucially, a kind of fear that the person is choosing and even enjoying. Think of someone on a roller coaster: they are scared, their heart is pounding, but they are also loving every second. That feeling — the mix of excitement and controlled fear — is a thrill.

This is why activities like bungee jumping, scary movies, or even high-stakes competition are described as "thrilling." The word carries the idea that a little bit of risk or fear, when it is safe or voluntary, actually intensifies the pleasure.

Example: "She loved the thrill of driving fast on an open road."
Common ways "thrill" is used as a noun

"A thrill of [something]" — Here, thrill describes a sudden rush of a specific feeling. You can have a thrill of excitement, a thrill of fear, a thrill of anticipation, or a thrill of joy.
Example: "A thrill of panic passed over him."

"The thrill of [an activity]" — This refers to what makes an activity exciting or worth doing.
Example: "Nothing could match the thrill of performing on stage."

"Get a thrill from/out of something" — This means that something gives you a powerful feeling of excitement.
Example: "She gets a real thrill out of solving difficult puzzles."

"What a thrill!" — Used as an exclamation to express that something was wonderfully exciting.

"A cheap thrill" — This is a slightly negative phrase. It refers to an excitement that is shallow, trivial, or comes from something not very admirable.
Example: "He seemed to get a cheap thrill out of embarrassing others."

"Thrills and spills" — A set phrase meaning the exciting and sometimes risky moments in an activity or event.
How thrill differs from similar words

Excitement is broader and more general. It can be mild or strong, slow-building or sudden, and it doesn't necessarily have a physical sensation. A thrill is always sudden, always intense, and always physical.

Joy is a deeper emotional state that can last a long time and is entirely warm and positive. A thrill is a spike — a brief intense moment, not a lasting condition.

A rush is very similar to a thrill (especially the adrenaline-driven kind), but "rush" leans more toward the physiological, energetic burst — like what you feel from adrenaline. A thrill is slightly more emotional and experiential in tone.

Exhilaration is what you often feel after a thrill — an energized, uplifted, almost breathless feeling that lasts a little longer. A thrill is the sharp moment; exhilaration is the glow it leaves behind.

Think of a thrill as the lightning bolt of human emotion. It is sudden, it is powerful, it travels through your whole body, and it is gone in a flash — but the memory of it stays. It can come from beauty, danger, achievement, surprise, or fear. It is always intense, never subtle. When you want to describe a peak moment of excitement — one that grips both your body and your emotions at the same time — the word you reach for is thrill.
15989:
To thrill means to cause — or to feel — a sudden, powerful wave of excitement, joy, or intense pleasure. It is not a quiet or gentle feeling. It is sharp, immediate, and strong. It hits you all at once.

When something thrills you, it does not just make you happy. It moves you deeply. It stirs something inside you in a way that feels almost electric.

This is important: thrill is not only an emotional word — it is also a physical one. When you are thrilled, you often feel it in your body. A shiver runs through you. Your skin tingles. Your heart beats faster. Your breath quickens. The word captures that exact moment when your whole body responds to something exciting or beautiful or extraordinary.

Think of a moment when you heard a piece of music that gave you goosebumps. Or when your team scored the winning goal in the last second. Or when someone told you news you had been desperately hoping for. That sharp, rushing, full-body wave of feeling? That is what it means to be thrilled.
How to Use It in Sentences

The verb "thrill" works in two main ways:

1. Something thrills someone.
Here, a thing or person causes the feeling of thrilling in someone else.

  • The singer's voice thrilled the entire audience.
  • The news of her promotion thrilled her family.
  • The final scene of the movie thrilled everyone who watched it.

In this pattern, the subject (the singer, the news, the scene) is actively producing the feeling of excitement in the object (the audience, her family, everyone).

2. Someone thrills to something.
Here, a person feels the thrill in response to something. This pattern is less common but used in more literary or expressive writing.

  • He thrilled to the sound of the crowd cheering his name.
  • She thrilled to every page of the adventure novel.
  • They thrilled to the sight of the northern lights.

Since you want full coverage, here are the most important forms of this verb:

Thrilled — the past tense and also a very common adjective meaning feeling great excitement or joy.

  • "I am thrilled to meet you." (extremely happy and excited)
  • "She was thrilled by the surprise party."

Thrilling — an adjective describing something that causes thrill; something that produces strong, exciting feelings.

  • "It was a thrilling race." (so exciting it gave you that rushing feeling)
  • "He told a thrilling story."

Thrills — third person singular present tense.

  • "Every great performance thrills the people who witness it."

"Thrill" sits at the intense end of the excitement scale. Compare:

  • Something can interest you — mild engagement.
  • Something can please you — gentle satisfaction.
  • Something can excite you — noticeable energy and enthusiasm.
  • Something can thrill you — a sudden, powerful, almost overwhelming wave of excitement and joy.

So when you choose "thrill," you are saying something stronger than simply "excite" or "make happy." You are saying the feeling was sharp, immediate, and deeply felt.
The Slight Edge of Danger or Suspense

"Thrill" also carries a fascinating secondary quality: it can include a small element of danger, suspense, or fear — but in an enjoyable way. Think about the word thriller (a genre of movies and books). The thrill there comes partly from tension and risk.

So "thrilling" can also describe something that is exciting partly because it feels a little dangerous or uncertain — a roller coaster, a tight sports game, a suspenseful movie, a daring adventure. The element of risk makes the excitement even sharper.

This means "thrill" can live in two slightly different emotional spaces:

  • Pure joy and excitement (thrilled by wonderful news)
  • Excitement mixed with a rush of tension or slight fear (thrilled by a risky adventure)

Both are correct, and both involve that same physical-emotional wave.
What Kinds of Things Thrill People?

To cement your understanding, here is a sense of the range of experiences this word covers:

  • A breathtaking live performance
  • An unexpected piece of wonderful news
  • A dramatic, last-minute victory in sport
  • Meeting someone you deeply admire
  • A dangerous but exciting experience like skydiving
  • A piece of music that is extraordinarily beautiful
  • A book or film so gripping it leaves you breathless
  • Witnessing something rare or magnificent in nature

Any experience that produces that sudden, powerful, body-and-soul response can be described with this word.

To thrill is to cause or feel a sudden, strong, electric rush of excitement, joy, or intense pleasure — one that is felt not just in the mind but throughout the body. It is a powerful word. When you use it, you are saying that something moved a person deeply, immediately, and intensely.
